analysis.one_liner: Blocks states from punishing people who travel out of state for reproductive health care.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2026 with 35 cosponsors, the bill to protect interstate travel for reproductive health care has had no committee action since its referral to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it unlawful for any person or government to restrict, punish, or disadvantage someone who travels to another state for reproductive health care that is legal where it happens, or anyone who helps them travel, such as friends, funds, employers, or doctors. It preempts state laws that get in the way, lets the Justice Department sue to stop enforcement, and lets patients and providers sue in court for damages and court orders. It does not pay for anyone's travel or medical care; it only bars interference.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live in states that restrict abortion or other reproductive care but travel to states where it is legal, along with the doctors, clinics, funds, and employers who help them. The bill would shield them from state penalties, give them the right to sue anyone who interferes, and let courts strike down conflicting state and local laws. Out-of-state patients would also gain equal standing with a state's own residents when they seek care there.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients traveling for reproductive care and their helpers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any person or government to restrict, sanction, discriminate against, or disadvantage anyone who travels to another state for reproductive health care that is legal in that state, or anyone who assists that travel.
Protects health care providers who serve out-of-state patients from being punished for providing services they lawfully offer their own residents.

Creates enforcement teeth: the Attorney General can sue states or officials who violate the law, and patients, helpers, and providers can file their own lawsuits for damages, court orders, and attorney's fees.
Preempts any state or local law that conflicts with the travel right, and waives state sovereign and official immunity so those laws can actually be challenged and struck down in court.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments that restrict abortion or other reproductive care would lose the ability to enforce those restrictions against people who travel, their helpers, and out-of-state providers, and would face lawsuits. Opponents of abortion travel would lose legal tools they currently use, including private civil enforcement. Taxpayers would bear the cost of Justice Department enforcement and litigation if the bill were enacted.
analysis.who_pays_short: State governments restricting reproductive care travel

drawbacks.text: The bill's enforcement design is unusually aggressive: it waives state sovereign immunity and officials' qualified immunity and preempts all conflicting state and local laws, which would invite immediate, years-long constitutional challenges if enacted.
It provides no money. A patient who cannot afford to travel out of state for care gains nothing from a law that only blocks interference with travel.

Its scope is very broad: it bars any 'disadvantage' by any person, lets providers sue on behalf of their patients, and requires courts to award the plaintiff's legal fees, which could generate extensive litigation over what counts as interference.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states that restrict reproductive care, the bill addresses a real, direct harm — being punished or cut off from legal care elsewhere — and its enforcement mechanism is strong enough to matter. The honest costs are that it would be challenged in court on the breadth of its immunity waiver and preemption, that it does nothing for people who cannot afford to travel at all, and that its broad language would be tested through years of litigation. Those are real limitations, but they are outweighed by the immediate protection it offers to patients and providers if it worked as written.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 8, 2026, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on June 8, 2026, with 35 original cosponsors: 34 of the 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 independents.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the bill's action history, with the session ending January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, state governments that restrict abortion-related travel keep their current laws and enforcement tools in place, and opponents of the bill have avoided any recorded vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States restricting abortion travel, so far

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 8, 2026 and has taken no action since — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

against.name: 55 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat or independent — 34 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — and not a single Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Reproductive health care providers (abortion and pregnancy-care clinics)
industries.note: The bill bars states from punishing providers for serving out-of-state patients and lets clinics sue on behalf of their staff and patients, with attorney's fees awarded to prevailing plaintiffs. That expands and secures their patient base across state lines.

industries.industry: State and local governments that restrict reproductive care
industries.note: Their laws restricting travel, punishing helpers, or targeting out-of-state providers would be preempted and unenforceable, and their officials could be sued individually with immunity waived.
Private civil suits and sanctions aimed at people who assist abortion travel would be barred, and defendants could remove such cases to federal court and recover fees in non-frivolous actions.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and not one Republican cosponsor, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup or a floor vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Bills that sit without committee action after referral typically die when the Congress expires and must be reintroduced from scratch.
